blocks.text: The first stored-program computer in New Zealand government is not a settled one-machine story. Treasury’s IBM 650 was installed in November 1960 and formally opened on 23 March 1961. A later study makes the case that an ICT 1201 for the Department of Education arrived earlier and was processing teachers’ pay by August or September 1960. That earlier date is plausible, but rests on a thinner record than the Treasury chronology.

blocks.text: The IBM 650’s first major job was a fortnightly payroll for about 34,000 public servants. It calculated entitlements and deductions, stored the results on magnetic tape, then produced pay vouchers and punched-card cheques. A. C. Shailes later recalled the practical cost of keeping the installation running: the machine room needed air conditioning, a raised floor for cabling and standby power.

blocks.text: These were batch systems. Staff prepared the cards or tape, queued a job, collected its output and checked the result before it went back into departmental work. By 1969 nine government departments had computers; Treasury and Education also ran bureau jobs for other departments. In 1970 much of that processing moved into a central government computer centre, while the Ministry of Works kept specialist engineering capacity.
